article.Citation/Title: Jensen, S. E., & Ramsay, R. (1963). Treatment of chronic alcoholism with lysergic acid diethylamide. Canadian Psychiatric Association Journal, 8(3), 182-188.
article.SourcePDF: alcohol/Jensen, S. E., & Ramsay, R. (1963). Treatment of chronic alcoholism with lysergic acid diethylamide.pdf
article.InterventionDescription: Single oral LSD-25 dose (~200 gamma, occasionally 400 gamma) given during the final week of a 2-month inpatient AA-oriented group-therapy program at Saskatchewan Hospital, Weyburn.

ae_events.Description: Confusion or amnesia with LSD doses above the routine 200 gamma, described as undesirable and sometimes disturbing when patients later try to affirm the experience's reality.
Intense anxiety, usually early in the session during abreaction of repressed material, and again if patients resist 'surrendering' during the transcendental experience.
Nausea occurring early in the LSD session, often alongside anxiety preceding abreaction of repressed material.
Emotional tension during the LSD session, described by the authors as a side effect that resolves with release after abreaction of repressed material.
Headache listed by the authors among the drug's side effects occurring around the abreaction phase of the LSD session.

article.Outcome: The article's Results section reports a single explicit inferential test: 'A chi-square test showed that significantly more of the alcoholics treated with LSD were dry or improved at the time of follow-up, than patients receiving group therapy alone or of the controls.' The dichotomization actually tested is dry-or-improved vs. unimproved. Counting: LSD-treated dry-or-improved = 39+7=46 of 62 followed up = 74.2% (rounds to 74%); controls dry-or-improved = 8+4=12 of 29 followed up = 41.4% (rounds to 41%). The article also separately breaks out a dry-only rate (39/62=63% LSD vs 8/29=27% control), but this narrower category is a descriptive component, not itself the category the printed chi-square test evaluated; the dry-or-improved dichotomy was chosen as Outcome because it is the one the authors' own stated inferential test addresses. This is a non-obvious judgment call — a reviewer could reasonably prefer the dry-only breakdown (63% vs 27%) instead.
article.SD: No chi-square statistic value or degrees of freedom is printed anywhere in the article; the authors state only that 'a chi-square test showed' the group difference, followed by a parenthetical p-value notation (captured in PVal). With no numeric test statistic to report, SD is coded '.'.
article.PVal: Printed exactly as '(P> .01)' immediately after the chi-square sentence. Transcribed verbatim as '>.01' per the non-fabrication rule against constructing a decoding theory for a number that looks internally inconsistent: the prose claims the LSD group was 'significantly' better, which conventionally implies P<.01, yet the printed inequality reads P>.01 (greater than, not less than). This is flagged as a likely typographical/OCR inversion of '<' vs '>', but the value is reported exactly as printed rather than silently corrected.
article.SampleSize_NFinal: 91 = 62 (LSD-treated patients followed up 6-18 months, of the 70 who received the full LSD programme, 8 lost to follow-up) + 29 (controls followed up, of 55 total, 26 lost to follow-up). This is the combined denominator underlying the 74%-vs-41% dry-or-improved comparison used in Outcome.

MethodologyDescribedYN.note: Met: objective (report of LSD-25 as adjuvant to psychotherapy for chronic alcoholics), design (2-month inpatient programme culminating in a single LSD session, compared against a non-LSD control group), setting (Saskatchewan Hospital, Weyburn, Alcoholic Unit), intervention (dosage, timing, therapist staffing described in detail), comparator (controls were patients admitted when no beds were available for the LSD group, receiving individual treatment by other psychiatrists), outcomes (dry/improved/unimproved categories with percentages), randomization (the text explains how the non-random control group arose — bed availability, not deliberate allocation — which is judged to satisfy 'described' even though the mechanism was not randomization), statistical_methods (chi-square test named), results (percentages and outcome counts given for both groups), and harms (drug effects — anxiety, nausea, tension, headache, confusion/amnesia — are explicitly named and discussed, even though reframed as therapeutic rather than tallied as formal AEs). Not met: eligibility (only a referral-source policy is described, 'their most severe or chronic cases,' with no formal inclusion/exclusion list), sample_size_power (no power calculation or sample-size justification anywhere), blinding (no statement about blinding, presence or absence, anywhere in the article), funding_coi (no funding source or conflict-of-interest statement found). n_met=10 < 13, so MethodologyDescribedYN=0.

article.Pos Result Y/N: Coded 1. The article states directly that 'significantly more of the alcoholics treated with LSD were dry or improved at the time of follow-up, than patients receiving group therapy alone or of the controls' — both the direction (74% vs 41% dry-or-improved) and the authors' own characterization support a positive result, independent of the printed P-value's ambiguous inequality direction (see PVal).
article.Clincial Trial YN: 1, consistent with the eligibility screen: a prospectively planned single LSD-25 administration ('part of a research programme carried out in Saskatchewan') delivered under a defined 2-month inpatient protocol with an assigned regimen (200 gamma, last week of stay) and prospective 6-18 month outcome assessment.
article.RandomizationYN: 0. The control group was formed by administrative circumstance ('patients admitted to the hospital at a time when no beds were available to the group'), not randomization. This is a genuine absence of randomization, not an inapplicable design element, so 0 rather than 3.
article.BlindingYN: 0. No blinding of any kind (patient, therapist, or rater) is described or implied anywhere in the article; treatment was open-label by nature (a therapist remains with the patient throughout the LSD session).
article.Comparator: 1. A non-randomized comparator group of 55 patients exists — those admitted when no beds were available for the LSD programme, who instead 'received individual treatment by other psychiatrists.' This is a naturalistic/administrative comparator, not a randomized or matched control, which is noted here as a design limitation.
article.Power: 0. No a priori or post hoc power discussion appears anywhere in the article.
article.Retention (%): 72.8 = (62 LSD followed-up + 29 control followed-up) / (70 LSD enrolled + 55 control enrolled) x 100 = 91/125 = 72.8%. The study is not randomized, so the enrolled N (not a randomized N) is used as the denominator per convention. Component counts ('eight were lost to follow-up' of 70; '26 lost to follow-up' of 55) are given directly in the Results section.
article.ConfoundYN: 0. The article notes that referred patients were generally severe cases ('their policy has been to refer their most severe or chronic cases to the Saskatchewan Hospital'), which is background/prognostic framing for the treated population as a whole, but no statistical adjustment, stratification, or explicit comparison of baseline severity between the LSD and control groups is performed or discussed. Judgment call — a reviewer could argue this framing constitutes a substantive discussion of a potential confound.
article.InclusionExclusionCriteria: 0. Only a referral-source policy is described (severity-based triage from the Alcoholic Counselling Centre in Regina); no formal inclusion or exclusion criteria (diagnostic criteria, comorbidity exclusions, age limits) for study entry are stated.
article.ValidatedScaleMeasYN: 0. Outcome is classified by follow-up interview into dry/improved/unimproved categories devised by the authors; no named validated scale or psychometric instrument (e.g., AUDIT, ASI) is used.
article.Funding/COI YN: 0. No funding source, grant support, or conflict-of-interest disclosure appears anywhere in the article text; only the presentation venue (Third World Congress of Psychiatry, 1961) and author affiliation are given.
article.BaseStatus: Coded 'Severe'. The Results section states the treated sample 'would be considered to have a very serious prognosis by all ordinary means of evaluation': 87% had failed Alcoholics Anonymous at least once, 24% were separated or divorced, and 57% had received prior psychiatric treatment, with patients specifically referred as the hospital's 'most severe or chronic cases.'
article.Age_Median: Bracket '30-50'. 'Their age varied from 24 to 65, most being between 30 and 45 and the mean age being 39.3' — the mean of 39.3 falls within 30-50.
article.PercentFem: Coded '.'. No aggregate percent-female figure is reported anywhere. All five illustrative case histories describe male patients ('he'/'him' throughout), which is suggestive but not a substitute for a reported sample-wide percentage; not inferred as 0 to avoid fabricating an unreported number.
article.RaceEthnicity_BIPOCPercent: Coded '.'. Race/ethnicity of the sample is never reported in aggregate; individual case histories mention ancestry incidentally ('English background', 'Irish sign painter') but no BIPOC percentage is given.
article.Country_USvsNonUS: NonUS. Treatment delivered at the Saskatchewan Hospital, Weyburn, Saskatchewan, Canada.
article.RecruitmentRepresentYN: 1, judgment call. Patients were routine referrals from the Alcoholic Counselling Centre in Regina and direct hospital admissions rather than research-recruited volunteers, reflecting a real clinical referral pathway. However, the stated referral policy specifically channels 'their most severe or chronic cases' to this hospital, which is itself a form of severity-based selection rather than a representative cross-section of all alcoholics in care; flagged for reviewer consideration.
article.HarmsAssessed: 1, required to agree with SafetyReported='Y' (see that entry for the underlying judgment call).
article.SafetyReported: Y, non-obvious judgment call. There is no dedicated Adverse-Events/Safety section, table, or systematic per-patient AE tally. However, the article explicitly names and discusses a category of drug effects as 'side effects of the drug — anxiety, nausea, tension, headache' (Abreaction section), and separately states that doses above 200 gamma produce 'confusion or amnesia' that is 'undesirable and sometimes even disturbing to the patient' (Treatment Programme section). Per the cardinal rule to distinguish 'no AEs occurred' and 'the authors never looked' from cases where effects were in fact observed and discussed, this narrative discussion is judged sufficient to satisfy the SafetyReported gate, even though the effects are reframed as therapeutic/expected rather than formally tallied as adverse events. A stricter reviewer could instead code 'N' given the absence of any formal harms-assessment methodology.
article.Followup in months: 18. The systematic cohort follow-up window used for the quantitative Outcome is stated as 'followed up between six and 18 months after discharge' for both the LSD-treated (N=70) and control (N=55) groups; 18 (the upper bound) is used as the longest systematic follow-up. Individual case histories separately report longer anecdotal single-patient follow-ups (e.g., Case 3: 'remained sober for two years'), but these fall outside the systematic 6-18-month cohort window used for the reported percentages, so they are not used to extend this field.
article.PhysicalChangeMeasured: 0. No biomarkers, physiological measures, or vital signs are reported as a measured outcome domain. The drug-effect discussion (confusion, amnesia, nausea, headache) describes intervention side effects captured under HarmsAssessed/AE fields, not a physical outcome measure administered as part of the study's outcome assessment.
article.MentalHealthChangeMeasured: 0, non-obvious judgment call. The article extensively narrates psychological and spiritual transformation (the 'transcendental experience,' surrender, humility, self-acceptance) as the therapeutic mechanism of the LSD session, but this is qualitative/narrative description of process, not a formally scored mental-health outcome instrument (e.g., a depression or anxiety scale) administered and reported as a study outcome.
article.ReductionMeasured: 1. The 'improved' category — 'were drinking, but definitely less than before' (7 LSD-treated, 4 control) — is a distinct partial-reduction outcome, separate from complete cessation.
article.CessationMeasured: 1. 'Remained dry continuously since discharge' is the complete-cessation outcome category (39 LSD-treated, 8 control).
article.RelapseMeasured: 1, judgment call. The dry classification explicitly accounts for 'a short testing bout of drinking immediately after discharge,' and the unimproved category tracks continued/returned drinking, indicating that return-to-use was tracked as part of follow-up classification, even though no distinct time-to-relapse metric is reported.
article.EligibleYN: Y. (a) Clinical trial: a prospectively planned single LSD-25 administration under a defined 2-month inpatient research programme, with an assigned regimen and prospective 6-18 month outcome assessment against a comparator group — passes. (b) SUD outcome: drinking status (dry/improved/unimproved) is the article's central reported outcome — passes.

ae_events.Jensen 1963_AE01: SeverityIndeterminate='Y'. The article states only that higher-than-routine doses (>200 gamma) produce 'confusion or amnesia' that is 'undesirable and sometimes even disturbing,' with no information on duration, whether it resolved within the session or persisted, or whether any intervention was needed. Absent such signals, defaulted to Mild per the under-specified-AE rule, flagged indeterminate rather than silently absorbed into a confident grade. Onset coded 'post-session-acute' because the text frames the difficulty as arising 'later, when he is trying to establish for himself the reality of the experience,' i.e. after the acute drug effect, though this too is imprecise.
ae_events.Jensen 1963_AE02: AE_type coded 'challenging_experience' rather than plain 'AE' because the anxiety described is explicitly framed by the authors as expected, in-session phenomenology tied to the therapeutic abreaction and 'surrender' process, consistent with the rubric's guidance that expected in-session anxiety/fear during dosing is CEQ-sense phenomenology graded by consequences rather than intensity. No intervention or persistence is described, and the text explicitly notes a 'release of emotional tension' following the abreaction, supporting a confident Mild grade (not indeterminate).
ae_events.Jensen 1963_AE03: Grouped by the authors with anxiety/tension/headache as 'side effects of the drug' occurring around the abreaction phase; no count or duration given beyond the implied in-session, transient nature of abreaction-related symptoms, supporting Mild with no intervention.
ae_events.Jensen 1963_AE04: Same grouped 'side effects' passage as AE02/AE03/AE05; the text explicitly states this resolves with 'a definite release of emotional tension' after abreaction, supporting a confident Mild, in-session grade.
ae_events.Jensen 1963_AE05: Same grouped 'side effects' passage; headache is listed alongside anxiety, nausea, and tension with no further detail, but the shared context (transient, early-session, resolves with abreaction) supports Mild without needing an indeterminate flag.

config_proposal.note: Article reports dry-or-improved status at 6-18-month follow-up for 46/62 (74%) LSD-treated patients vs 12/29 (41%) non-randomized controls, the exact dichotomy the authors' own chi-square test evaluated ('significantly more...were dry or improved'), though no chi-square value was printed (only a p-value notation, itself internally ambiguous — see PVal rationale). Per instruction to compute an odds ratio from two-group proportions where the counts support one: OR = (46x17)/(16x12) = 782/192 = 4.07, oriented toward the LSD-favorable direction (no sign flip needed). Confidence is 'approx' rather than 'clean' because this is a proportion-to-odds-ratio conversion from a non-randomized (bed-availability) comparator, which the framework explicitly flags as an approx-triggering assumption.
